learn: Lexical semantics: lemmas, senses and polysemy
Word relations: synonymy, similarity, relatedness, antonymy, hypernymy, meronymy
Dot product vs cosine similarity, with worked numbers
Dense embeddings, self-supervision and the embedding lookup
intro.why: Representing words as vectors is the foundation of modern NLP: retrieval, classification, Word2Vec, language models, Transformers and RAG all start from turning words into numbers whose geometry reflects meaning.

sections.title: Lexical semantics: lemmas and senses
sections.plain: What a word 'means': a dictionary form can have several senses.
sections.body:
To build systems that answer questions or hold conversations we need a theory of word meaning: lexical semantics. Naive approaches fail: representing words as arbitrary indices (word #4271) says nothing about meaning, and the purely logical approach ("the meaning of dog is DOG") just renames the problem.

  • Lemma (citation form): the dictionary headword, e.g. "mouse" for "mice".
  • Sense: the specific meaning of a lemma in context. "mouse" has a rodent sense and a computer-device sense: polysemy.

Why it matters: a question answerer must know that "How tall is Mt. Everest?" is answered by "The official height of Mount Everest is 29,029 ft" (tall ≈ height); plagiarism detection must catch reworded text.

sections.title: Word relations: synonymy, similarity, relatedness
sections.plain: Words can mean the same, be alike, be associated, be opposite, or sit in hierarchies.
sections.body:
• Synonymy: (nearly) the same meaning, substitutable without changing truth: couch/sofa, big/large, automobile/car. Perfect synonymy is rare: "my big sister" ≠ "my large sister"; "H₂O" and "water" differ in register.
  • Similarity: words are alike in meaning: coffee/tea, car/bicycle.
  • Relatedness (association): words co-occur in the same scene or frame without being similar: coffee/cup, doctor/scalpel.
  • Antonymy: opposites on one feature: hot/cold, rise/fall (otherwise very similar!).
  • Hypernymy (is-a): animal > dog > poodle.
  • Meronymy (part-of): wheel / car.

sections.title: Connotation and affective meaning
sections.plain: Beyond literal meaning, words carry emotional colour.
sections.body:
WordDenotationConnotation
homea place where one liveswarmth, safety, family
cheaplow in costnegative: poor quality, stingy
inexpensivelow in costpositive: good value
slimhaving little fatpositive: fit, elegant
skinnyhaving little fatnegative: unhealthy

Affective meaning varies along three dimensions (Osgood et al., 1957): valence (pleasantness), arousal (intensity of emotion) and dominance (degree of control). Connotation is the foundation of sentiment analysis, and it is one of the things good word vectors capture.

sections.title: The distributional hypothesis
sections.plain: You shall know a word by the company it keeps.
sections.body:
Distributional hypothesis (Firth, 1957; Harris, 1954): words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings.

Ongchoi. Seen in "ongchoi is delicious sautéed with garlic", "ongchoi is superb over rice", "ongchoi leaves with salty sauces", while "spinach sautéed with garlic over rice" and "chard stems and leaves are delicious" share the same contexts. We infer ongchoi is a leafy green, without a definition.

Vector semantics makes this computable: represent a word as a point in a multi-dimensional space derived from its contexts (an embedding). Benefits: generalisation (similar words, similar vectors, so a model trained on "car" helps with "automobile"), dimensionality reduction, and mathematical operations (similarity, analogies).

sections.title: Term-document and term-term matrices
sections.plain: Count words per document, or words near other words.
sections.body:
Term-document matrix: rows = words, columns = documents.

As You Like ItTwelfth NightJulius CaesarHenry V
battle10713
good114806289
fool365814

"battle" = [1, 0, 7, 13]; a play's vector is its column. "fool" is a comedy word, "battle" a history/tragedy word. Foundation of information retrieval.

Term-term (word-word) matrix: dimensions are context words within a window (e.g. ±4):

computerdataresultpiesugar
cherry28944225
strawberry0016019
digital167016838554
information33253982378513

Such count vectors are long (|V|, e.g. 50,000 dimensions) and sparse (mostly zeros).

sections.title: Dot product and cosine similarity
sections.plain: Measure the angle between vectors, not their length.
sections.body:
The dot product $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf w = \sum_i v_iw_i$ is high when vectors are large in the same dimensions, but it favours long vectors: frequent words have large counts everywhere, so the dot product conflates frequency with similarity. Normalise by length:

$$\cos(\mathbf v,\mathbf w) = \frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf w}{|\mathbf v||\mathbf w|} = \frac{\sum_i v_iw_i}{\sqrt{\sum_i v_i^2}\sqrt{\sum_i w_i^2}}$$

1 for the same direction, 0 for orthogonal, −1 for opposite (counts are non-negative, so 0 to 1 here). Worked (ex1): cos(digital, information) = 0.996, cos(cherry, strawberry) = 0.969, cos(cherry, information) = 0.019. Yet dot(cherry, information) = 44,443 exceeds dot(cherry, strawberry) = 27,004, purely because "information" is frequent.

sections.title: TF-IDF and PMI weighting
sections.plain: Damp huge counts and reward words that are rare across documents.
sections.body:
Raw frequency is paradoxical: frequent co-occurrence is informative ("sugar" near "apricot"), but extremely frequent words ("the", "it") are everywhere and say little.

$$\text{tf}_{t,d} = \log_{10}(\text{count}(t,d)+1),\qquad \text{idf}_t = \log_{10}\frac{N}{\text{df}_t},\qquad w_{t,d} = \text{tf}_{t,d}\times\text{idf}_t$$

Worked. "the" 1,000 times: tf = log₁₀ 1001 ≈ 3.0; "data" 10 times: tf ≈ 1.04 (the gap shrinks from 100× to 3×). With N = 100 documents: df = 5 → idf = log₁₀ 20 = 1.30; df = 100 → idf = 0 (a word in every document can't discriminate).

For word-word matrices the analogous weighting is pointwise mutual information, $\text{PMI}(w,c) = \log_2\frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)P(c)}$: how much more often w and c co-occur than if independent; PPMI clips negatives to 0.

sections.title: Dense embeddings and self-supervision
sections.plain: Short learned vectors (50–300 numbers) beat long sparse counts.
sections.body:
Dense vectors have 50–300 dimensions with mostly non-zero values, learned rather than counted. They generalise better (synonyms share dimensions instead of being separate columns), need fewer parameters in downstream models, and capture similarity and analogies.

Prediction instead of counting. Train a classifier on a fake task, "is word c likely to appear near word w?", and keep its learned weights as embeddings. Running text supplies the labels for free: self-supervision. For "the quick brown fox jumps", (fox, brown) is a positive pair; (fox, keyboard) a sampled negative. This is Word2Vec (M3).

One-hot vectors and the embedding matrix. A one-hot vector has a single 1 at the word's index among V zeros. The embedding matrix $W \in \mathbb R^{V\times D}$ has one D-dimensional row per word; multiplying a one-hot vector by W just selects that row: the lookup trick, so no actual multiplication is needed.

Code example ex2: from a 6-sentence corpus, PPMI + a 2-dimensional SVD places cat/dog together (cosine 1.0) and stock/prices together, orthogonal to the pets (cosine ≈ 0).

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Similarity vs relatedness in vectors: small context windows favour similarity (substitutable words), large windows or document contexts favour relatedness (topical association).
  • Antonyms look similar in distributional vectors because they occur in the same contexts ("hot coffee", "cold coffee"); separating them needs extra signals.
  • Bias: embeddings learn societal stereotypes present in text (gender–occupation associations); debiasing and auditing are active areas.
  • Static vs contextual: one vector per word type can't distinguish senses; contextual embeddings (BERT, M11) give each occurrence its own vector.

code.title: TF-IDF, PPMI and dense SVD vectors
code.explain: Reproduces the tf and idf worked values, computes tf-idf on a 6-document corpus, then builds a windowed co-occurrence matrix, applies PPMI and keeps 2 SVD dimensions as dense embeddings.
mistakes: Using raw counts instead of PPMI before SVD.
Expecting meaningful embeddings from a tiny corpus beyond toy illustrations.
code.notes: Truncated SVD of PPMI (LSA-style) is a count-based route to dense vectors; Word2Vec is the prediction-based route.
code.code:
"""TF-IDF weighting, PPMI, and dense vectors from a truncated SVD of a co-occurrence matrix."""
import numpy as np, math
print("log TF: 'the' x1000 ->", round(math.log10(1001), 2), "; 'data' x10 ->", round(math.log10(11), 2))
for df in (1, 5, 50, 100): print(f"idf with N=100, df={df:>3}: {math.log10(100 / df):.2f}")

corpus = ["the cat sat on the mat", "the dog sat on the log", "a cat chased a dog",
          "stock prices rose sharply", "the market and stock prices fell", "investors sold stock"]
docs = [d.split() for d in corpus]; vocab = sorted({w for d in docs for w in d}); N = len(docs)
tf = np.array([[math.log10(d.count(w) + 1) for d in docs] for w in vocab])
df = np.array([sum(w in d for d in docs) for w in vocab]); idf = np.log10(N / df)
tfidf = tf * idf[:, None]
for w in ("the", "cat", "stock", "prices"):
    i = vocab.index(w); print(f"tf-idf row '{w}': {np.round(tfidf[i], 2)}  (df={df[i]})")

# word-word co-occurrence within each sentence, then PPMI
idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}; C = np.zeros((len(vocab),) * 2)
for d in docs:
    for i, a in enumerate(d):
        for j, b in enumerate(d):
            if i != j and abs(i - j) <= 2: C[idx[a], idx[b]] += 1
P = C / C.sum(); pw = P.sum(1, keepdims=True); pc = P.sum(0, keepdims=True)
with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    ppmi = np.maximum(0, np.nan_to_num(np.log2(P / (pw * pc)), neginf=0))
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(ppmi); E = U[:, :2] * S[:2]                # 2-D dense embeddings
def cos(a, b): return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b) + 1e-12)
for a, b in [("cat", "dog"), ("stock", "prices"), ("cat", "stock")]:
    print(f"dense 2-D cosine({a}, {b}) = {cos(E[idx[a]], E[idx[b]]):+.2f}")
